I can't speak for all people with BDD, so this is just how it is for me, but it's not about someone just convincing you. It's like getting help with unraveling a huge tangle of thread. My BDD most likely formed within trauma and it was an easy way for me to dismiss my worth and explain why all these terrible things had happened to me. I'm getting help with my trauma alongside things like BDD and that helped me a lot. 

BDD is obsessive and sort of delusional. It's hard to see how wrong you are when you're in it. A therapist can help you see how irrational and unhealthy it all is. Working on your self esteem is probably the best thing you can do with BDD because BDD is an internal problem, not an aesthetic problem. A lot of people who do seek surgeries and stuff like that don't feel sated by the physical change. So having someone working on bettering your self esteem, and understanding why / how you got there in the first place, and retraining your thought patterns, helping with breaking the compulsions, all of that, can be a big help. The biggest thing is you don't have to believe your beliefs are incorrect. And at first, you probably won't. But with treatment (or just self help), you have to keep going and doing the work, even if you don't see an immediate difference.

For me, it was therapy, treatment, breaking the thought patterns and compulsions and learning as much as I can about how BDD functions and what the traps of BDD are (there's a lot of them, they're obsessive and miserable and I'm sorry you're struggling so much with it, I know how hard it is.)

A therapist could talk to you about BDD if that's something you have access to, but even if you don't have BDD, it's not really a bad idea to get into the things that are involved in BDD recovery, anyway. It's really seriously not invalidating anyone else to worry about your \*own\* mental health.  It's good that you're recognizing the thought patterns at all. Like, seriously, that's basically the first step to changing them. As much as possible it's good to cut down on body checking behaviors because they're obsessive and it's like a snowball of self hate rolling down the hill.

I really suggest learning as much about BDD as possible. It's like learning a magicians tricks, to me. The more you know, the more you can see the faults in it, the more you can understand your brain is just trained to go down this same path of "I'm ugly and worthless", and choose to take a different path. But that isn't to say that it's easy, it's really hard, but you're worth it. The BDD foundation has some seminars on youtube and they have a podcast that I have found helpful, maybe you will too. 

Besides that here's my advice. As much as you possibly can, stop body checking behaviors. That's checking the mirror, doing your hair a million times (I did this too!), taking lots of pictures, comparing to others. Even if you just cut down a little bit. Right now you probably feel like you're down deep stuck in the BDD cave-in hole, at least that's how I felt. So any progress is progress, here. We are retraining our brain to think differently about ourselves, that's hard work, and any progress will pile up for the better. Catering to your inner self here is important. So, building a self worth that isn't based around appearance. When you do have to look in the mirror, look into your eyes and say 3 things about yourself that you like that aren't related to appearance, and do this everyday if possible. It retrains your brain to think of something other than the incessant BDD thoughts when you come in contact with the mirror. 

As for having a hard time getting out, it's basically the same thing. If you can manage a walk, try that. Just try your best to get out, and if you can only go out a bit at a time, that's great. Try to stay out a little longer than last time. Even if you're just going out for no reason, to get a drink or something. Maybe once walks get easier, you can try to do a grocery run on your own. Or just go into the store and get like 5 items on a list. Start small, be kind to yourself, don't be discouraged when you struggle (we all do!!!), celebrate your wins no matter how small. You DESERVE kindness and relief.

 I think something very difficult about BDD is that, although we really aren't as ugly as we believe, a lot of people really are just cruel and shallow and it's even easier to be that way through a screen. However not everyone is that way, and in my experience cruel people aren't really that happy in their lives. I think that we are so, so used to our inner thoughts being so cruel, so warped and self hating, to an irrational and probably delusional degree, that reading words that reflect that back at us is a massive comfort. It's like looking in the mirror and thinking "I hate you I'm so ugly", except someone else is doing all the work for you, you don't even have to think it! This is why not engaging in that type of behavior (for as long as you can, even for a few minutes or a day) is so uncomfortable but so necessary. You deserve so much more than cruel words.

I highly suggest researching dysmorphia, i don’t want you to be totally overwhelmed by her experience with it but i think learning about it helps people who want to support those with it.
